title: Paul Graham: Why being good works as startup strategy (Startup School 08)
summary: Graham argues that "make something people want" plus "don't worry about money early" describes something that looks like a nonprofit, and that successful startups often behave that way. Benevolence boosts morale, attracts help and talent, and works as a decision compass. Startups should launch fast and stay hard to kill.

principles.text: Make something people want; money is easier than making something great, so defer the business model.
principles.quote: Don't worry too much about money. Um, not because it's not important, but because it's so much easier than making something great.

principles.text: Very successful startups often behave like nonprofits, and nonprofit ideas often make good companies.
principles.quote: Very successful startups often behave like nonprofits. And when you think about nonprofit ideas, surprisingly often, they'd make good companies.

principles.text: When small you can't bully users, so you must charm them; being nice is how you grow.
principles.quote: When you're small, you can't bully your users, so you have to charm them.

principles.text: Use "do what's best for your users" as the compass for the thousands of decisions a startup faces.
principles.quote: Just do whatever is best for your users, right? You can hold on to that like a rope in a hurricane and it will save you if anything can.

principles.text: Launch quickly so users exist to take care of; serving them forces you to learn what they want.
principles.quote: as soon as you launch the Tamagotchi effect kicks in. Once you have users to take care of you're forced to figure out what they want and that information is actually very valuable.

principles.text: Commitment plus cheap operations makes a startup very hard to kill, which also impresses investors.
principles.quote: If you're really committed and your startup is cheap to run, you become very hard to kill.
